Fugue in C Major, BWV 547 Rhetorical

The organ fugue that Scott Roberts (2004, chapter 7) uses to show combining forces as a notable property. The subject is one bar long and seems to modulate, so it cannot stand alone; its entries come in groups of three that Roberts calls Exposition Blocks. The blocks shrink from three entries to two to one, and in the last two blocks the raised 4 that pulled the subject toward G gives way to a natural 4.

  • 72 bars, alla breve
  • 4 voices, 5 from m. 50
  • 12 Exposition Blocks, 30 block entries
  • Over 50 statements in all
  • Properties reconciled

The Six Steps

Roberts reports this analysis as a narrative and gives no full annotated score, since his figures cover nearly every bar. The sorting into cards is ours ours.

  1. STEP 1

    Identify the Traditional Fugue Elements

    Mark every entry, countersubject, codetta, episode and coda, with voice, key and devices.

    • A one-bar subject, and more than 50 statements: upright, inverted, augmented and overlapping.
    • The opening runs subject, answer, subject, then a codetta and an answer, not the usual order.
    • The pedal first enters in m. 49; from m. 50 there are five voices.
  2. STEP 2

    Find the Notable Properties

    Look for core material: here a single subject is too slight, so groups of entries take its place.

    • A brief subject, one bar long.
    • It seems to modulate through ♯4, yet subject and answer together never really leave C.
    • Entries in threes: the Exposition Blocks (EBs), the integrants of this fugue.
  3. STEP 3

    Look for Patterns in the Sections

    Measure the sections: do they grow, shrink, mirror or form simple ratios?

    The blocks narrow: 3 entries each through EB 7, then 2 from EB 8, and a single entry in EB 12. The first narrowing, in m. 49, splits the fugue 2:1 (48 + 24 bars), and the block entries split 21:9, that is 7:3.

  4. STEP 4

    Test Other Segmentations

    Cut the fugue another way when the traditional sections do not serve.

    The traditional exposition does not fit: the fourth entry ends over a weak chord. Roberts replaces entries and episodes with blocks and digressions (Table 10); this is the departure from traditional segmentation the chapter argues for.

  5. STEP 5

    Repeat the Pattern Search

    Look for patterns again in the new segmentation.

    In the block structure: the narrowing 3 → 2 → 1, the 2:1 split at m. 49, and the progression of devices from EB 8 on, augmentation, plain entries, augmented inversion, half-length overlap, a single entry.

  6. STEP 6

    Decide How the Fugue Responds

    A property is reconciled when it returns with the trait that made it notable, now completed. All reconciled: rhetorical.

    Rhetorical. The blocks fuse until one entry can stand alone, and in EB 11 the subject keeps 4 natural and stays in C. Both resolutions work together at the end.

Narrowing Blocks

Entries per Exposition Block (Table 10). Blue: the first part of the fugue; orange: from m. 49.

2:1 and 7:3 Roberts

The first reduction, from three entries to two, falls in m. 49, splitting the 72 bars into 48 and 24, a 2:1 ratio. Bach marks the moment with the first entrance of the pedal and the start of augmentation. The block entries divide the same way, 21 before and 9 after: 7:3.

30 or 50? Roberts

Table 10 counts 30 entries because it leaves out every statement outside a block: inversions in the digressions, inversions used as countersubjects and stray entries. With those the fugue has over 50.

Notable Properties

Roberts’s numbered list from the opening, plus the raised 4 he discusses later. The buttons scroll the score to the place and play it.

1 · Structural unit

A one-bar subject

Why notable
Very short, and open at the end. With so many entries, the subject alone is too slight to serve as core material.
Role
It is the reason the entries combine into blocks.
2 · Linear tendency

The raised 4 that seems to modulate

Why notable
F♯ at the end of the subject tonicizes G. In the tonal answer the same place falls on B, the leading tone of C, which pulls back to the tonic. So subject and answer together never really leave C.
Reconciled
EB 11 (m. 68): the answer comes first and the subject that follows keeps 4 natural, staying in C.
3 · Combining forces

Entries in groups of three

Why notable
From the start, entries arrive in threes; the exposition itself ends with the third entry’s V chord. These Exposition Blocks are the integrants, separated by digressions.
Reconciled
The blocks narrow to two entries (EB 8 on) and then to one (EB 12), a tonal answer that can now stand alone.
Indicator

Entries hidden by their number

Why notable
Some 49 statements and constant strettos make single entries count for little, as in BWV 545.
Role
Points the analyst away from the entries toward the blocks and the raised 4.

Blocks and Digressions

Roberts’s Table 10 with where each section starts (measure.beat) and how long it lasts. ▶ plays the section.

SectionStartsBarsKeysComments

Keys follow Table 10: a subject entry is named by the key it starts in and “modulates” from; a tonal answer by the key it returns to. In print Roberts tells them apart by underlining, which the plain text here cannot show.

Kneading the Blocks

From Three to One Roberts

From m. 49 the blocks are worked over step by step. EB 8 drops to two entries, augmented, as a fifth voice joins. EB 9 returns to plain entries. EB 10 augments and inverts them. EB 11 overlaps its two entries by half their length, and EB 12 is a single entry, a tonal answer leading to the final tonic.

Roberts compares this stretching, shrinking and turning over to kneading bread: the separate entries are worked into one whole.

Inversions Change Jobs Roberts

In the first part of the fugue the inverted subject (sometimes modified) fills the digressions. Later the same inversions accompany the block entries as countersubjects. From the start, entries also overlap by one note, the last note of one serving as the first of the next.

Two Resolutions Together Roberts

The natural 4 of EB 11 and the single entry of EB 12 arrive together, and the fugue ends with them, as in his other rhetorical fugues.

About This Score

Notes and Layout

The score is engraved from Peter van Kranenburg’s Humdrum encoding of BWV 547. It is the only machine-readable source found so far, so the notes are still to be checked bar by bar against the Bach-Gesellschaft edition (BG 15, 1867). Roberts quotes the Neue Bach-Ausgabe IV/5; bar numbers agree.

Each line of the encoding has its own staff (open score); Bach’s layout has two manual staves and pedal. In mm. 47–48 the encoding puts a held G5 in its lowest line, so it shows on the pedal staff although the pedal cannot reach it; this is one of the places to check against the print.

Playback uses recorded samples: the Steinway Grand by default, an Italian harpsichord at A = 415, or a baroque pipe organ at Chorton A = 465 with pedal pipes for the pedal.

What Is Roberts and What Is Ours

  • Roberts The Exposition Blocks, digressions, codettas and keys (Table 10), the properties, the 2:1 and 21:9 ratios, the treatment of the blocks from EB 8 on (Figures 35–39) and the rhetorical verdict.
  • ours Which notes form each block entry and the other statements (matching, one by eye); the sorting into six steps; bracket placement and where the m. 8 cadence sits in the bar.
